title: Paper-Level Computerized Adaptive Testing for High-Stakes Examination via Multi-Objective Optimization

problem.claim: Question-level computerized adaptive testing creates comparability, implementation-cost, and multi-factor balancing challenges in standardized high-stakes examinations.

gap.claim: Existing CAT systems primarily use question-level adaptation suited to practice scenarios rather than high-stakes standardized examinations.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Paper-level Computerized Adaptive Testing, which adaptively assigns test papers of varying difficulty across multiple stages based on earlier-stage performance.
It formulates paper assembly in PCAT as a population-based multi-objective optimization problem.
It proposes a corresponding evaluation method for PCAT.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that paper-level adaptation preserves adaptability while improving comparability because later questions depend only on earlier-stage performance.
The authors report that offline cognitive diagnosis and paper assembly eliminate exam-time real-time interactions and reduce the burden of maintaining a large-scale CAT system.
The authors report that population-based multi-objective optimization produces multiple high-quality solutions in one run for frequent standardized-exam administration.

narrative_sequence.summary: CAT estimates proficiency with relatively few questions, but existing systems generally adapt at the question level.
Question-level adaptation presents comparability, implementation-cost, and balancing challenges in high-stakes standardized examinations.
The authors introduce PCAT, a staged paper-level adaptive mechanism, together with an evaluation method.
PCAT solves paper assembly using population-based multi-objective optimization and moves intensive processing offline.
The authors describe improved comparability, reduced real-time interaction, and lower system-maintenance burden as benefits of PCAT.

unknowns: No quantitative experimental results, datasets, baselines, or evaluation outcomes are supplied.
The specific multi-objective formulation, optimization procedure, and evaluation protocol are not described.
The supplied abstract unit ends mid-sentence, so the final claimed advantage is incomplete.
